keywords: Slack off / be idle cessō, cessāre, cessāvī, cessātum Ancient Latin cessō, cessāre, cessāvī, cessātum — be idle, delay, loiter or stop doing something; the context determines whether this means shirking. labōrem neglegō — neglect my work; sēgniter agō — act sluggishly; ōtiō mē dēdō — give myself over to idleness. langueō, languēre, languī — be weak or languid; it does not by itself imply deliberate shirking. The earlier languēō incorrectly lengthened a vowel before another vowel. Nōlī cessāre. — Don’t dawdle / stop slacking. Tōtum diem cessat. — He idles all day / has been idling all day.

keywords: Accountability / hold oneself accountable ratiōnem reddere Classical idiom Descriptive extension ratiōnem reddere — give an account or answer for one’s conduct; ratiōnem factī suī / factōrum suōrum reddere — account for one’s own action or actions. putāre / arbitrārī sibi ratiōnem reddendam esse — think oneself answerable; agnōscere sibi ratiōnem reddendam esse — acknowledge that one must give an account. These are descriptions of self-accountability using the Classical construction. Cicero, Verr. 2.2.28: semper ita vīvāmus, ut ratiōnem reddendam nōbīs arbitrēmur . ratiōnem ab aliquō reposcere — demand an account from someone; Caesar, BG 5.30: abs tē ratiōnem reposcent . Both passages are cited under ratiō in Lewis & Short. sibi imputāre — attribute something to oneself; culpam in sē recipere / culpam agnōscere — accept or acknowledge blame. These imply more than neutral answerability. cūram suscipere / in sē recipere — undertake responsibility prospectively. Modern respōnsābilitātem assumere / suscipere is a broader expression and is not a uniquely exact equivalent for self-accountability. Ulixēs nōn agnōscit sibi dē eō quod accidit ratiōnem reddendam esse; culpam sociīs tribuit. — Odysseus does not acknowledge himself answerable for what happened; he assigns blame to his companions.
